case_studies.title: LeapQuant: Efficient Linear Attention with Accurate Recurrent State Quantization
case_studies.abstract: Recent LLMs increasingly adopt hybrid designs that replace standard attention with linear attention, such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). Although they compress the context into a fixed-size recurrent state and substantially reduce the cost of long-context processing, repeatedly reading and updating that state remains a major inference bottleneck. Quantization offers a natural way to reduce this cost, but can significantly degrade model quality, due to the accumulation of rounding errors and the presence of outlier rows and columns in the state. To address these challen
case_studies.summary: LeapQuant introduces a new way to quantise the recurrent state used in linear attention models, cutting the cost of repeatedly updating that state while keeping model accuracy. The authors built a lightweight quantisation framework that avoids rounding errors and handles outliers, achieving faster inference on large‑context LLMs.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a specialized quantization technique for linear attention in large language models, which could appeal to engineers working with LLM deployments seeking inference efficiency. However, the work is highly technical and specific to model internals rather than infrastructure or DevOps tools. The immediate practical applicability within 90 days is limited, as the method would require integration into existing model frameworks and substantial testing before deployment. Thus, while novel, its direct IT relevance and near-term actionable value are modest.

case_studies.title: $S^3$: Spectral Null-Space Swap Makes Reasoning Models Efficient
case_studies.abstract: LLMs trained with Chain-of-thought excel in reasoning capability, but often come with excessive token cost. We find that the core of reasoning capacity lies in the Thinking model's weight component within the null space of a projection defined by the corresponding Non-thinking model's dominant singular directions, and removing the subspace component can largely improve reasoning efficiency without hurting the accuracy gained during thinking-mode post-training. Unlike existing efforts that mostly operate within the dominant subspace, we are the first to unveil the critical role of the null spac
case_studies.summary: This research shows that by swapping out a small part of a large language model’s weights – the part that lies in the null space of a projection defined by a related model – you can reduce the token cost of chain‑of‑thought reasoning without losing accuracy. They built a method that identifies and removes these null‑space weight components and tested it on several reasoning tasks, finding a significant efficiency gain. For typical cloud infrastructure managers, this work is not directly relevant to everyday operations.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a novel technique to reduce token consumption for chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs, which could translate into cost savings on cloud-based inference. However, the work is theoretical and does not provide an actionable implementation or direct impact on current IT infrastructure, tooling, or DevOps pipelines. Therefore, IT relevance and immediate value for engineers are modest.

case_studies.title: SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving
case_studies.abstract: No single way of parallelizing attention serves large language models well under all loads. Low concurrency favors tensor parallelism, many independent requests favor data-parallel attention, and long prompts favor context parallelism. Reasoning, agentic, and RL-rollout workloads make a fixed choice untenable: a batch that begins as many short requests ends as a few very long ones, so the best layout changes while the same requests run. Serving engines nevertheless fix one layout at launch, because changing it has meant draining requests and restarting workers. We present SPLASH, a serving sys
case_studies.summary: SPLASH lets you change the way an LLM splits its attention workload (tensor, data, or context parallelism) on the fly, matching the mix of short and long requests in real time. It builds a lightweight controller that monitors request patterns and reconfigures the parallel layout without draining traffic or restarting servers. The result is smoother scaling and lower latency across mixed workloads, especially where request lengths shift during a session.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM serving, here is what to do: 1) add SPLASH’s controller to your inference stack to monitor request length and batch size; 2) configure it to automatically switch between tensor, data, and context parallelism based on defined thresholds; 3) enable zero‑downtime handoff so workers keep processing while the layout updates. This flags a risk: if your org uses a static parallelism setting, check whether the request mix varies over time and consider adopting SPLASH to avoid performance dips.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a dynamic attention-parallelism switching mechanism (SPLASH) that adapts to varying request workloads in LLM serving. This is novel from an engineering standpoint, as it addresses a real pain point in managing large-scale LLM deployments across cloud environments. For IT engineers dealing with AWS/Azure hosting, SSO, and endpoint management, the ability to auto‑switch between tensor, data, and context parallelism without draining traffic is directly applicable to improving throughput and reducing costs. The technique can be incorporated into existing serving frameworks (e.g., Triton, TorchServe) or cloud‑managed LLM services, enabling immediate automation of resource allocation and performance tuning, thus offering tangible value within 90 days. Consequently all three criteria score high, resulting in a total score of 90.

case_studies.title: EASE: Behavior-Adaptive Skill Curation for Self-Evolving Agents
case_studies.abstract: Agent skills provide a lightweight mechanism for self-evolving agents to accumulate reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. However, existing learned skill curators typically optimize curation without explicitly modeling downstream executor behavior. We show that this can cause systematic cross-executor degradation: curators trained with different executors perform best when paired with their own training executor, indicating that effective skill curation is executor-dependent. We formulate behavior-adaptive skill curation and introduce EASE, a framework that learns a
case_studies.summary: EASE tackles the problem that AI skill curators often pick skills that work well only with the specific executor they were trained on, leading to poor performance when paired with other executors. It builds a behaviour‑adaptive skill curator that learns to pick skills based on the current executor’s behaviour, reducing cross‑executor performance loss. The result is a more robust agent that can switch between different executors without losing efficiency. This is not directly relevant to typical cloud infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a novel framework (EASE) for behavior-adaptive skill curation in self-evolving agents, which is a fresh concept within AI agent development. It has limited direct relevance to everyday IT infrastructure tasks such as SSO, endpoint management, or cloud operations, but could inform future automation tooling and agentic systems that might be deployed in enterprise environments. Practical applicability within 90 days is modest, as the work is primarily research-oriented and would require significant engineering effort to integrate into existing IT workflows.

case_studies.title: CounterSteer: Suppressing Indirect Prompt Injection with Activation Steering
case_studies.abstract: Indirect prompt injection makes an LLM agent treat untrusted retrieved text as instructions. We present CounterSteer, an inference-time defense that suppresses this behavior inside the model. Per model, a five-step recipe fits a residual-stream direction from paired episodes differing only in whether an embedded instruction is followed, and retains it only if it passes pre-specified causal and capability gates. At deployment, the direction is subtracted from every tool-result token during prefill. The edit is always on--there is no detection decision to evade--and requires no fine-tuning, auxi
case_studies.summary: CounterSteer blocks an LLM from acting on untrusted text that looks like instructions, preventing indirect prompt injection. It builds an inference‑time filter that learns a direction to subtract from model outputs, using only a few examples and no fine‑tuning. The result is a safer model that ignores malicious instruction cues while still performing normally.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, check whether your LLM‑based services might feed untrusted data as tool results; if so, apply a CounterSteer‑style vector subtraction to each response to block indirect instructions, following the three‑step recipe: (1) generate paired episodes with and without embedded instructions, (2) learn the residual direction and gate it, (3) subtract the direction from every token during prefill. This reduces injection risk without extra training.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a novel inference-time defense against indirect prompt injection, which is a relevant security concern for LLM deployments. However, the technique is highly technical and does not directly translate to immediate operational changes in typical IT infrastructure or DevOps workflows. It offers limited actionable steps for IT engineers, yielding a modest 90‑day value score. The combined score exceeds 40, so the signal is considered useful.

case_studies.title: Towards an AI Software Factory for Data Systems
case_studies.abstract: AI-assisted coding tools deliver significant acceleration of coding, but only limited impact across the end-to-end software development lifecycle (SDLC)--an Amdahl's law effect! In this paper, we discuss our progress towards building an AI SW Factory that accelerates all the stages of SDLC-Targeting, Coding, Reviewing, and Ops. The AI SW Factory produces a metadata exhaust that enables self-improvement by fine-tuning model weights and updating our World Model (a rich data substrate). We focus on Data Systems and the important class of Evolutionary Coding Tasks (i.e., those with a measurable ob
case_studies.summary: This research tackles the slow, manual stages of software development by building an AI‑driven Software Factory that speeds up target definition, coding, reviewing and operations for data systems. The team produced a system that generates detailed metadata, which it uses to fine‑tune its models and update a World Model, leading to quicker, higher‑quality code and smoother operational hand‑off. The result is a more automated, self‑improving SDLC that cuts cycle time and reduces human error.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, use the AI SW Factory to auto‑generate deployment scripts and configuration files: 1) feed your current data‑system specs into the factory, 2) let it produce IaC and CI/CD pipelines, 3) integrate the output into your existing Ops workflow and monitor for performance regressions.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes an AI‐driven Software Factory aimed at accelerating all stages of the SDLC for data systems, including Targeting, Coding, Reviewing, and Ops. This directly touches on areas that UK IT engineers manage (cloud deployments, MLOps, automation pipelines). The concept of generating a metadata exhaust to enable self‑improvement of models could influence how teams structure CI/CD, model monitoring, and infrastructure provisioning. Although the abstract is incomplete, the described approach offers actionable ideas (e.g., automating code reviews, generating deployment artifacts, and continuous fine‑tuning) that could be prototyped within 90 days. It also hints at potential security implications of auto‑generated code and model drift, which is highly relevant. The novelty score reflects the introduction of a holistic, AI‑centric SDLC workflow, while the relevance and value scores are moderate to high because of the potential for rapid experimentation in existing cloud and DevOps environments.
